title: Stack, Heap & Object Lifetime
html:
Where an object lives decides how long it lives. C++ has four storage durations; knowing them is the key to avoiding dangling pointers.

Memory segments of a process

RegionHoldsLifetimeManaged by
StackLocal variables, parameters, return addressesUntil the enclosing block endsAutomatic (push/pop)
Heap (free store)Objects from new / containers' buffersUntil deleteYou (or RAII owners)
Static / global dataGlobals, static locals & membersWhole programRuntime
Code (text)Machine instructions, string literals (read-only data)Whole programLoader

Storage durations

  • Automatic — block-scoped locals. Destroyed in reverse order of construction when the block ends.
  • Static — globals, namespace variables, static locals/members. Static locals are initialised on first use (thread-safe since C++11).
  • Dynamic — new/delete, or owned by smart pointers/containers.
  • Thread — thread_local variables: one instance per thread.

Stack vs heap

StackHeap
Allocation speedVery fast (move a pointer)Slower (allocator bookkeeping)
Size limitSmall (~1–8 MB)Large (up to available memory)
LifetimeTied to scopeExplicit / owner-controlled
FragmentationNonePossible
Typical failureStack overflow (deep recursion, huge local arrays)Leaks, use-after-free
Watch out

int big[10'000'000]; as a local variable (40 MB) overflows the stack. Use std::vector<int> big(10'000'000); — the vector object sits on the stack, its buffer on the heap.

Object size & alignment

Key point

Members are laid out in declaration order with padding to satisfy alignment. Ordering members from largest to smallest often shrinks a struct. An empty class still has size 1 so distinct objects have distinct addresses.

Why is the stack faster than the heap?

Allocating on the stack is just adjusting the stack pointer, and freeing is automatic at scope exit; the memory is also hot in cache. Heap allocation must find a free block of the right size (and possibly lock for thread safety), then later return it.

In what order are local objects destroyed?

In reverse order of construction, when control leaves their scope — whether by reaching }, return, break, or an exception unwinding the stack. This deterministic order is what makes RAII reliable.
